newsitem.title: LEBANON: Germany to examine toxic waste in Beirut-official.
newsitem.headline: Germany to examine toxic waste in Beirut-official.

text.p: A German expert will examine some 680 tonnes of plastic waste illegally shipped to Beirut with the aim of taking them back, a minister of Lebanon's outgoing cabinet was quoted as saying on Friday.

"The authorities in Baden-Wuerttemberg...have appointed a German expert who is expected to arrive in Beirut soon to examine the containers and prove they are polluted," the official National News Agency quoted outgoing environment minister Pierre Pharaon as saying.

He said Lebanon's efforts have led to the "intervention of the German government with the aim of taking the 36 containers back to Germany." Pharaon was speaking hours before Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri announced a new 30-member government.

But in Germany a spokesman for the Baden-Wuerttemberg state environment ministry, which is handling the matter there, told Reuters: "We have sent a letter to Beirut asking the authorities to give us the reasons why they would like us to take the waste and provide some proof of what exactly it consists of."
He said it was by no means established either that the waste came from the plant in Philippsburg where it is supposed to have originated, or that it was actually contaminated and hazardous.
"Once Beirut provides the information, it is possible the ministry might send its own experts to look at the shipment -- but this is still quite a way down the road," he added.

Lebanese judicial authorities on Wednesday charged seven people -- a German, a Dutchman, four Lebanese men and a German-based Jordanian businessman -- with involvement in "importing 36 containers of plastic waste contaminated with poisonous chemical compounds" from Germany to Beirut.
If convicted, they face up to five years in jail with hard labour.

International environmental watchdog Greenpeace said the German, Bernd Bretzing, was the manager of Hagen-based RC Reifenrecycling which it had said was one of two German firms that shipped the waste to Beirut.
Greenpeace said some of the waste was contaminated with chemical compounds like pesticides and fertilizers, and some of it was biologically-contaminated hospital waste.
